strengths: The unified representation addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: combining objects, interactive parts, spatial and functional relations, and affordances could support more detailed embodied reasoning than object-centric graphs.

OP3DSG combines sensible design choices: object-conditioned part prompts, color-assisted multi-view association, and geometry-informed language reasoning. The method builds coherently on appropriately cited detection and scene-graph approaches.

The reported retrieval improvements are substantial. Part-node R@3 reaches 83.6 versus 52.4 for the strongest baseline, while functional-triplet R@3 improves from 41.9 to 51.1. Updating several baselines to GPT-5 helps control for language-model improvements.

Table 5 provides useful component ablations, and Table 4 explicitly examines stricter localization criteria. UniGraph3D's annotation consolidation and added relationships could also provide a useful evaluation resource.
weaknesses: The principal part-grounding claim is weakened by Table 4. Part-node recall falls from 83.6 under nonzero-IoU matching to 25.8 at IoU≥0.10 and 13.0 at IoP≥0.25, below KeySG's 30.4 and 23.4. These results suggest that strong semantic retrieval does not yet establish accurate localization of actionable components, which is central to the motivation.

The evaluation does not substantiate reduced hallucinations or improved precision. Tables 2–5 report recall, without edge precision, false-positive rates, or graph-size controls. The embedding-based matching protocol also leaves candidate vocabularies, duplicate handling, instance assignment, and affordance-to-node matching insufficiently specified. Strong top-K phrase retrieval alone cannot establish physically correct graph predictions.

The claimed verification gate is insufficiently defined. Section 4.4 describes LLMs checking geometric consistency, but does not specify an independently enforced acceptance rule or provide an ablation isolating verification from candidate pruning and agent decomposition. Language-only world knowledge also cannot reliably distinguish actual remote-control or power connections from plausible category-level relationships.

Attribution of the gains remains incomplete. OP3DSG introduces a detector pretrained for part segmentation alongside its knowledge base and fusion changes, but the comparisons do not hold the perception backbone fixed across methods. Table 5 supports the utility of several components, yet does not determine how much improvement comes from the proposed framework versus stronger pretrained part perception. As an Algorithms/General contribution, the methodological advance beyond integrating existing components needs clearer isolation.

UniGraph3D is small—251 object nodes and 414 part nodes—and its validation is underdocumented in the supplied manuscript. Scene counts, evaluation splits, annotation agreement, and the separation between knowledge-base curation and evaluation scenes are not reported. The manually curated object–part vocabulary is not accompanied by tests on unseen objects or parts, leaving the extent of open-vocabulary generalization uncertain.

Efficiency and downstream impact are asserted more strongly than demonstrated. There are no runtime, token-cost, memory, or scene-size scaling measurements; placing a graph in a single prompt does not itself establish scalability. Section 6 provides illustrative robot applications without trial counts, success rates, or comparisons demonstrating the benefit of part-aware graphs.

Reproducibility is limited by missing knowledge-base contents, prompts, geometric relation rules, association thresholds, and histogram settings in the supplied material. There is also a concrete inconsistency in Eq. (1): retaining pixels only when saturation is high AND intensity is low rejects more than the simultaneously overexposed and weakly chromatic pixels described in the text. This is a correctable issue, but the implemented rule and handling of achromatic parts need clarification.

strengths: The unified representation addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: connecting objects, interactive parts, spatial and functional relations, and affordances for embodied reasoning. The motivation and pipeline are clearly presented.

The reported retrieval improvements are substantial. OP3DSG achieves 83.6% part-node R@3 versus 52.4% for the strongest baseline in Table 2, and improves functional and spatial triplet R@3 over OpenFunGraph++ by 9.2 and 7.9 percentage points, respectively.

Table 5 provides useful component ablations. Knowledge-guided prompting, color features, geometric context, and separate reasoning agents each contribute to the reported results. Updating several baselines to GPT-5 also addresses an important potential confound.

UniGraph3D adds useful annotations to attributed existing datasets, and the localization sensitivity study candidly exposes limitations that the main retrieval metrics obscure. The robot demonstrations illustrate plausible applications.
weaknesses: The central claim of precise part grounding is insufficiently supported. Main results require only non-zero 3D IoU. Under IoU≥0.10, part R@3 falls from 83.6% to 25.8%, below KeySG's 30.4%; under IoP≥0.25, it reaches only 13.0% versus KeySG's 23.4% (Table 4). OP3DSG also trails KeySG on overall IoP recall. These results materially qualify claims of geometrically stable interaction anchors and superior grounding.

Reduced hallucination and improved precision are asserted without direct measurements. The evaluation reports recall, which does not establish suppression of spurious edges. Section 4.4 describes LLM-based consistency checking but does not specify an independently enforced verification gate or isolate verification in an ablation. Edge precision, invalid-relation rates, and a controlled verification comparison are needed to substantiate this central claim.

Efficiency and scalability remain untested. There are no runtime, token-cost, memory, or graph-size scaling results. Processing associated pairs in a single prompt does not itself establish scalability, and all three agents independently refine spatial relations. The single-agent ablation also lacks matched inference budgets, leaving the benefit of task decomposition partly confounded with additional computation.

The empirical scope and benchmark documentation are insufficient for the breadth of the claims. UniGraph3D contains 251 object nodes and 414 part nodes, but the supplied manuscript does not report scene counts, evaluation splits, annotation agreement, or variation across scenes and runs. Important annotation details are deferred to supplementary material absent from the supplied PDF. Generalization beyond these consolidated indoor datasets is therefore difficult to assess.

The scope of open-vocabulary part recognition is unclear because candidate parts come from a predefined, empirically curated knowledge base. Its contents, coverage, construction protocol, and separation from evaluation categories are unspecified, and unseen object–part combinations are not evaluated. Moreover, comparisons do not hold the part-specialized detector and candidate vocabulary fixed across methods, so the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed fusion and reasoning mechanisms.

Reproducibility is limited by missing prompts, association thresholds, histogram settings and weights, geometric relation rules, and precise retrieval matching conventions. The nine-category affordance evaluation relies on top-K phrase similarity without establishing physically correct grounding. A smaller technical inconsistency also needs correction: Eq. (1) excludes pixels that are either low-saturation or high-value, whereas the prose says only pixels satisfying both conditions are discarded.

The real-world evidence is qualitative: Section 6 supplies no trial counts, success rates, baseline comparisons, or controlled evidence that part-aware graphs improve execution. The illustrated planning tasks do not establish reliable handle/button interaction. Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the useful integration and strong semantic retrieval results are outweighed by unresolved evidence gaps around grounding, verification, scalability, and generalization.

strengths: The unified representation addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: connecting objects, interactive parts, spatial and functional relations, and affordances in one grounded graph. Its relevance to embodied reasoning is well motivated.

OP3DSG combines complementary components coherently: object-conditioned part prompts, part-aware multi-view association, and geometry-conditioned LLM reasoning. The contribution has value as an integrated framework even though many individual components build on established methods.

The retrieval improvements are substantial. On UniGraph3D, part-node R@3 reaches 83.6 versus 52.4 for the strongest baseline; functional and spatial triplet R@3 reach 51.1 and 52.4 versus 41.9 and 44.5. Updating several baselines to GPT-5 helps establish that these gains are not simply due to a newer language model.

UniGraph3D adds useful annotations and canonicalizes inconsistent labels in existing resources. Table 5 also provides informative component ablations, while the localization sensitivity study transparently exposes an important limitation.
weaknesses: The evidence for precise part grounding is considerably weaker than the headline retrieval results suggest. The main metric accepts any nonzero 3D IoU. With IoU ≥ 0.10, part-node recall is only 25.8, below KeySG's 30.4; with IoP ≥ 0.25, it is 13.0 versus 23.4. This directly limits the central claim of geometrically stable interaction anchors. The paper acknowledges localization difficulty, but its broader claims about fine-grained grounding and robotic usefulness need qualification.

Reduced hallucination and improved precision are central claims, but Tables 2–5 report recall rather than precision, false-positive rates, or graph accuracy at controlled prediction budgets. These results cannot establish that spurious edges are suppressed. A separate ablation of the verification step and direct measurement of incorrect relations would be needed to substantiate that mechanism.

The open-vocabulary part capability depends on a manually curated object–part knowledge base whose coverage and construction are insufficiently specified in the supplied manuscript. There is no evaluation on held-out object–part combinations or categories outside this resource. The large degradation without knowledge in Table 5 makes this dependence especially consequential; open-vocabulary object recognition alone does not establish generalization of the complete part-aware system.

The comparisons do not isolate the benefit of the proposed pipeline from adopting a detector pretrained for part segmentation. Matching GPT versions is useful, but a baseline using the same detector and candidate prompts with standard fusion and relation reasoning would more clearly establish the additional methodological contribution.

The benchmark and implementation descriptions leave important reproducibility questions unresolved. Table 1 contains only 251 object and 414 part nodes, while scene counts, evaluation splits, annotation agreement, knowledge-base independence, and several matching details are deferred or unspecified. Exact prompts, association thresholds, histogram settings, and verification/integration procedures are also needed. The supplied PDF contains no supplement resolving these issues.

Scalability and downstream effectiveness are illustrated rather than adequately measured. There are no runtime, token-cost, memory, or scene-size scaling experiments, and the robot demonstrations provide no trial counts, success rates, or comparison against object-only graphs. Overall, the strong retrieval gains make this a close decision, but the evidence does not yet sufficiently support the central claims about reliable grounding, hallucination reduction, and scalable embodied use.

strengths: The unified representation addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: connecting objects, interactive parts, spatial and functional relations, and affordances. This is a useful extension of object-centric scene graphs for embodied reasoning.

The pipeline is coherent and practically motivated. Object-conditioned part prompts, color-assisted multi-view association, and geometry-initialized relation reasoning target identifiable failure modes. Table 5 provides evidence that each component contributes under the proposed evaluation protocol.

Reported retrieval improvements are substantial. Part-node R@3 reaches 83.6 versus 52.4 for KeySG, and functional-triplet R@3 reaches 51.1 versus 41.9 for OpenFunGraph++. Updating baselines to GPT-5 helps rule out language-model version alone as the explanation. Supplementary results on ReplicaSSG provide useful evidence beyond the unified benchmark.

UniGraph3D adds useful annotations to attributed source datasets and harmonizes functional labels. The manuscript also reports stricter localization results and concrete failure cases involving fragmentation, reflections, and false remote-control detections, providing valuable transparency.
weaknesses: The strongest results do not establish the precise part grounding central to the motivation. Main node retrieval requires only non-zero 3D IoU. Under the stricter criteria in Table 4, part R@3 falls from 83.6 to 25.8 at IoU≥0.10 and 13.0 at IoP≥0.25, below KeySG's 30.4 and 23.4, respectively. Overall IoP performance also trails KeySG, 31.4 versus 37.0. These results materially qualify claims of geometrically stable interaction anchors; the narrative that geometric superiority extends across both criteria is too broad.

The evaluation does not adequately test the claimed suppression of hallucinated relations. Only recall is reported, without precision, false-positive rates, or graph-size statistics. Functional labels are reduced to 11 categories and affordances to nine, making high-K retrieval relatively permissive. Top-1 results, class-balanced metrics, and triplet evaluation with stronger endpoint localization would better establish useful graph correctness. Affordance evaluation also needs a clearer account of spatial instance matching, since it explicitly ignores node-label correctness.

The source of the gains is insufficiently isolated. OP3DSG introduces VLPart pretrained on part-centric data, whereas the baseline extensions primarily add prompts and newer language models. There is no controlled comparison giving a strong baseline the same detector and candidate vocabulary, nor a reasoning comparison on identical ground-truth nodes. The ablations support the complete pipeline but cannot establish how much improvement comes from the proposed fusion and reasoning versus stronger perception. Algorithmic originality therefore remains less well demonstrated than the integration contribution.

The central 'verification-gated' reasoning mechanism is underspecified. Section 4.4 describes LLMs checking geometry through prompts, but supplies neither the actual prompts nor an explicit acceptance rule or independent verification procedure. The supplement also omits the object–part knowledge base, several fusion parameters, and details resolving attachment among nearby objects of the same class. The finite curated knowledge base may constrain part coverage; no held-out object/part-combination evaluation establishes generalization beyond that coverage.

Benchmark documentation is insufficient for a convincing standalone benchmark contribution. Although UniGraph3D contains 251 objects and 414 parts, the manuscript does not clearly report its scene count, development/evaluation separation, annotator agreement, or quality-control process. It is also unclear whether knowledge-base curation and parameter selection used the evaluated scenes. The label-frequency plots show substantial imbalance, but no per-class results or uncertainty estimates are supplied. These omissions limit confidence in broad generalization without implying that leakage occurred.

Efficiency and robotic utility remain preliminary. Table 6 reports perception-stage memory and model-call counts, but no end-to-end latency, token costs, or scaling measurements; fewer calls alone do not establish scalability when prompts grow with graph size. Robot applications are qualitative demonstrations without trial counts, success rates, or comparisons showing the benefit of part-aware graphs. The integration and retrieval gains are promising, but these evidential gaps, together with the localization and evaluation concerns, favor rejection under the default Algorithms/General criteria.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: representing objects, actionable parts, spatial and functional relations, and affordances together. This unified representation is well motivated for embodied reasoning.

The reported retrieval improvements are substantial. On UniGraph3D, OP3DSG achieves 86.2% part-node R@5 versus 54.1% for KeySG, and 64.5% functional-triplet R@5 versus 45.9% for OpenFunGraph++. Comparisons using GPT-5 for the baselines help control for language-model improvements.

Table 5 provides useful component ablations: knowledge-guided prompting, color-based association, graph initialization, and separate reasoning agents each improve the reported metrics. Supplementary evaluations on the source datasets and ReplicaSSG provide additional evidence beyond the merged benchmark.

UniGraph3D adds potentially useful spatial and affordance annotations to attributed existing resources. The stricter localization evaluation and supplementary discussion of fragmentation, reflections, and false detections are valuable disclosures.
weaknesses: The evidence for accurate part grounding is considerably weaker than the headline retrieval results suggest. The main metric accepts any nonzero 3D IoU. In Table 4, part-node R@3 falls from 83.6% to 25.8% at IoU ≥ 0.10 and to 13.0% at IoP ≥ 0.25; KeySG achieves 30.4% and 23.4%, respectively. Thus, OP3DSG does not outperform the strongest comparator on either stricter part-localization measure. This matters directly to the claimed stable interaction anchors and precision needed for physical interaction. Corresponding triplet and affordance evaluations under stricter localization are missing.

The evaluation does not substantiate the central claim of suppressing hallucinations and improving precision. Results primarily report recall, without edge precision, false-positive rates, or a direct evaluation of the verification step. Top-5 and top-10 relation retrieval are also permissive given the 11 canonical functional labels. Section 4.4 describes LLM checks rather than a precisely specified constraint-enforcement procedure, so physical consistency is not guaranteed by the method as presented.

The open-vocabulary part-level claim needs qualification and stronger validation. Part candidates come from a manually curated object–part knowledge base, and parent assignment relies on object names appearing within part labels. The manuscript does not provide the knowledge base, its coverage, its construction relative to evaluation scenes, or results on unseen object–part combinations. Open-vocabulary object recognition alone does not establish generalization of this constrained part pipeline.

Important methodological details remain unspecified, including the actual reasoning and baseline prompts, verification and agent-output integration rules, association thresholds, histogram settings, and EMA coefficient. The supplementary material identifies models and some weights, but does not close these gaps. The ablations support the complete pipeline, yet do not cleanly isolate the benefit of the part-pretrained detector from the proposed processing, or verification from graph initialization and additional LLM computation.

The benchmark is small—251 object nodes and 414 part nodes—and its annotation reliability is insufficiently documented. The manuscript does not adequately specify scene selection, annotation staffing, independent checks, agreement, or validation of the canonical relation mappings. The affordance protocol is also unclear about spatial correspondence when scoring independently of node labels. These omissions limit confidence in the benchmark as a reproducible measure of grounded relational understanding.

Efficiency and robotics claims exceed the supplied evidence. Table 6 reports perception-stage memory and coarse call counts, but no end-to-end latency, token cost, or scaling with scene size; using one prompt per reasoning role does not establish scalability as graph inputs grow. The robot examples demonstrate integration, but provide no trial counts, success rates, or controlled comparison showing that part-aware graphs improve execution. As an Algorithms/General submission, the promising integration and retrieval gains are outweighed by these unresolved validation concerns.

strengths: The unified representation addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: connecting object and part perception with spatial relations, functional dependencies, and affordances. This is well motivated for embodied tasks requiring more detailed scene understanding than object-centric graphs provide.

OP3DSG combines sensible, complementary components: object-conditioned part prompts, color-assisted multi-view association, and geometry-initialized relational reasoning. The integration is practically useful even though many individual components build on established methods.

The reported retrieval improvements are substantial. On UniGraph3D, part-node R@3 reaches 83.6 versus 52.4 for the strongest baseline, while functional-triplet R@5 reaches 64.5 versus 45.9. Updating competing methods to GPT-5 helps establish that these gains are not simply attributable to the language-model version.

Table 5 provides useful component ablations, including reasoning comparisons with unchanged node predictions. Additional results on the constituent datasets and ReplicaSSG broaden the evidence beyond the merged benchmark.

UniGraph3D contributes harmonized annotations and additional spatial and affordance information, with attribution to its source datasets. The stricter localization evaluation and supplementary failure examples are valuable disclosures.
weaknesses: The evidence for precise part grounding is substantially weaker than the headline retrieval results suggest. The main metric accepts any nonzero 3D IoU. Under Table 4's stronger criteria, part R@3 falls from 83.6 to 25.8 at IoU ≥ 0.10 and 13.0 at IoP ≥ 0.25, below KeySG's 30.4 and 23.4. Although the paper acknowledges this limitation, it directly affects the central motivation of reliably grounding small interaction targets. Relation evaluation under stronger endpoint-localization criteria would help establish whether the graph gains survive this limitation.

Reduced hallucination and improved precision are central claims, but the reported quantitative metrics measure recall. They do not establish whether OP3DSG produces fewer false nodes, duplicate instances, or spurious relations. Top-3/top-5 semantic retrieval also offers limited evidence of exact relation and affordance correctness, especially with only 11 functional-relation and nine affordance categories. Precision/F1 and top-1 results are needed to substantiate these claims.

The reasoning contribution is insufficiently specified and isolated. Section 4.4 describes geometry verification largely as instructions to LLM agents, without providing exact prompts, explicit acceptance rules, or an ablation specifically disabling verification. The split-agent ablation changes decomposition and inference resources together. It therefore supports the complete configuration, but does not cleanly establish that verification gates suppress hallucinations or that decomposition itself explains the improvement.

Open-vocabulary generalization and reproducibility remain uncertain. Part candidates depend on a manually curated knowledge base whose contents, coverage, construction procedure, and separation from evaluation categories are not supplied. There is no held-out object/part evaluation. Association thresholds, several feature-extraction settings, and detailed graph-construction rules are also missing. The knowledge-base ablation demonstrates its importance, making these omissions consequential.

The benchmark is relatively small—251 object nodes and 414 part nodes—and its annotation reliability is not established through annotator agreement or an audit. Scene counts, development/evaluation separation, and detailed matching rules are insufficiently documented. A baseline using the same part detector and knowledge prompts would also help distinguish improvements from stronger perception inputs versus the proposed fusion and reasoning design.

Efficiency and robotics evidence support feasibility more strongly than the broader deployment claims. Table 6 reports perception-stage memory and approximate model-call counts, but no end-to-end latency, token cost, or scaling measurements. Robot applications provide illustrative demonstrations without trial counts, success rates, or comparison against object-only graphs; the pictured manipulation tasks do not directly test the claimed advantage for interacting with handles or buttons. Overall, the promising retrieval gains make this a close decision, but the grounding and evaluation concerns leave a slight preference for rejection.
